thread.title: Dow Jones, Apple Stock Rise As Xi Shelves Made In China 2025 In Win For Trump

author: JED GRAHAM
title: Dow Jones, Apple Stock Rise As Xi Shelves Made In China 2025 In Win For Trump
text:
A report that China will replace its Made in China 2025 plan for dominating advanced technology industries helped give the Dow Jones industrial average and broader stock market a boost Wednesday.
X
The move to carve out a bigger role for foreign companies is an essential concession for reaching a trade deal with the U.S. and provides more confirmation that President Trump is winning the China trade war. Apple ( AAPL ) stock joined in the Dow relief rally after a report that the iPhone maker and suppliers would mull a production shift out of China if Trump hits it with 25% tariffs.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 0.6% on the stock market today . Apple, a Dow Jones component, rose about 0.3%, while the Nasdaq added 1%.
On Monday, a Chinese court slapped a temporary ban on sales of some older Apple iPhones, which may have been more than a coincidence as Huawei is essentially on trial in the West. The action initially sent the Dow Jones and Apple stock reeling and offered a reminder that Beijing can seriously hurt U.S. companies using China as a manufacturing base and relying on it as a source of revenue.

On Tuesday, Trump said he is prepared to intervene on behalf of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou, who awaits extradition to the U.S. in connection with Iranian sanctions violations. Meanwhile, Beijing moved to follow through on its commitment to remove its extra 25% tariff on U.S.-built autos, leaving the rate at 15% for now.
The signs of progress come despite fear on Wall Street that Canada's arrest of one of China's most prominent corporate executives could snarl negotiations.
In reality, Huawei's precarious situation is like a Trump card in the U.S. negotiating hand. Huawei, China's leading technological hardware company, is dependent on chip technology from Qualcomm ( QCOM ) and the Android operating system from Google parent Alphabet ( GOOGL ).
Likewise, China also depends on leading-edge chip-equipment technology developed by Applied Materials ( AMAT ), Lam Research ( LCRX ) and KLA-Tencor ( KLAC ).
In other words, President Xi Jinping's Made in China 2025 plan would be dealt a dramatic setback if the conflict with the U.S. escalates. That explains why Beijing is now taking all the right steps to defuse the trade war. Trump undoubtedly wants a deal that will narrow the massive U.S. trade gap with China and deliver economic dividends to American agriculture and other industries. A deal will likely happen.
But New U.S. Sanctions Expected Yet the possibility of anything approaching a full resolution of the issues at the heart of the U.S.-China conflict — intellectual property rights, market openness, the skewed trade balance, cybertheft, territorial claims — remains a long shot because there is so little trust between the countries.
Even as China makes all the right moves, those moves are sure to be met with skepticism. The Washington Post reported that the Justice Department is getting ready to announce the indictments of hackers suspected of working for a Chinese intelligence service and participating in a long-running espionage campaign that targeted U.S. networks. More U.S. sanctions on alleged Chinese perpetrators are expected to be forthcoming, A whole host of such announcements are apparently coming.
Even with a trade agreement, the risk is rising that the global economy — especially high-tech sectors — will become divided between spheres of influence in a technological U.S.-China cold war. The U.S. wants to keep China's Huawei out of 5G next-generation mobile networks, citing security risks. China, through funding Belt and Road infrastructure projects in Asia, the Middle East and Africa, is working to expand its sphere of influence.
While a trade deal would undoubtedly be a good thing for the global economy in the near term, risk and uncertainty for American companies like Apple and other Dow Jones stocks may continue to rise.
Trump tariffs, though potentially damaging for both economies, have become a sideshow in the U.S.-China trade war. The real fight is over global leadership in advanced technology industries. A big question is whether the U.S. will move ahead with strict export controls on key technologies.
The more that the U.S. takes steps to impede Beijing's technology ambitions, the less of a future U.S. companies will have in China — no matter what today's big trade thaw news says.
